rules.title: The Core Rule
rules.concept: A singular subject takes a singular verb (with '-s'). A plural subject takes a plural verb (without '-s').

examples.incorrect: The students of this batch learns very quickly.
examples.correct: The students of this batch learn very quickly.

rules.title: The "Of" Trap (Prepositional Phrases)
rules.concept: Do not look at the noun right before the verb. Look for the real subject before the word "of".

examples.incorrect: The quality of these mangoes are not good.
examples.correct: The quality of these mangoes is not good. (Subject is 'quality', not 'mangoes')

rules.title: The "With" Family
rules.concept: When phrases like as well as, along with, together with, with, accompanied by, in addition to connect two subjects, the verb agrees only with the first subject.

examples.incorrect: The teacher, along with her students, were present.
examples.correct: The teacher, along with her students, was present.

rules.title: Either / Or and Neither / Nor (Proximity Rule)
rules.concept: When subjects are joined by either... or or neither... nor, the verb agrees with the nearest subject (the one closest to the verb).

examples.incorrect: Neither the manager nor the employees was present.
examples.correct: Neither the manager nor the employees were present.

rules.title: Each and Every
rules.concept: Words like Each, Every, Everyone, Someone, Nobody, Anyone are always singular and take a singular verb.

examples.incorrect: Each of the boys have a laptop.
examples.correct: Each of the boys has a laptop.

rules.title: The "One of the" Structure
rules.concept: The formula is: One of + Plural Noun + Singular Verb.

examples.incorrect: One of my friends are a doctor.
examples.correct: One of my friends is a doctor.

rules.title: One of the + Relative Pronoun (Who/Which/That)
rules.concept: If "who", "which", or "that" comes after the plural noun in the "one of" structure, the verb becomes plural because it refers to the whole group.

examples.incorrect: He is one of those men who tells lies.
examples.correct: He is one of those men who tell lies.

rules.title: A Number of vs. The Number of
rules.concept: A number of + Plural Noun = Plural Verb (means 'many'). The number of + Plural Noun = Singular Verb (means 'a specific total count').

examples.incorrect: A number of students has failed.
examples.correct: A number of students have failed.

examples.incorrect: The number of accident cases have increased.
examples.correct: The number of accident cases has increased.

rules.title: Collective Nouns (Jury, Team, Committee)
rules.concept: If the group works together as one body, use a singular verb. If the members are fighting or acting individually, use a plural verb.

examples.correct: The jury is giving its verdict. (United)
The jury were divided in their opinions. (Divided)

rules.title: Sums of Money, Distance, and Time
rules.concept: When a specific amount of money, distance, or time is thought of as a single lump sum, it takes a singular verb.

examples.incorrect: Ten miles are a long distance to walk.
examples.correct: Ten miles is a long distance to walk.

rules.title: Many a / More than one
rules.concept: The phrase "Many a" or "More than one" is always followed by a singular noun and a singular verb.

examples.incorrect: Many a students have failed the exam.
examples.correct: Many a student has failed the exam.

rules.title: Nouns that look plural but are singular
rules.concept: Names of subjects (Physics, Mathematics), games (Billiards, Darts), and diseases (Measles, Rickets) take a singular verb.

examples.incorrect: Mathematics are a difficult subject.
examples.correct: Mathematics is a difficult subject.

rules.title: "Nothing but"
rules.concept: When a sentence starts with "Nothing but", the verb must always be singular, whether the noun is singular or plural.

examples.incorrect: Nothing but trees were seen in the valley.

rules.title: Sentences starting with "There" or "Here"
rules.concept: In these sentences, the real subject comes after the verb. Check that noun to decide if the verb should be singular or plural.

examples.incorrect: There is many problems in this city.
examples.correct: There are many problems in this city.

rules.title: Two nouns making one unified dish/concept
rules.concept: When two nouns combine to form one single idea or dish (Bread and butter, Rice and curry, Slow and steady), they take a singular verb.

examples.incorrect: Bread and butter are my favorite breakfast.
examples.correct: Bread and butter is my favorite breakfast.

rules.title: Uncountable Nouns (Never use 's' or 'es')
rules.concept: Nouns like Scenery, Furniture, Advice, Information, Luggage, Baggage, Poetry, Hair are uncountable. You cannot make them plural by adding 's'. They always take a singular verb.

examples.incorrect: The furnitures of my house are new.
examples.correct: The furniture of my house is new.

rules.title: How to count uncountable nouns
rules.concept: To count words like advice or information, use phrases like "a piece of" or "pieces of".

examples.incorrect: He gave me two advices.
examples.correct: He gave me two pieces of advice.

rules.title: Nouns that are always Plural in form
rules.concept: Tools or clothing items with two symmetric parts (Scissors, Trousers, Pants, Spectacles, Binoculars, Tongs) are always plural and take a plural verb.

examples.incorrect: Where is my scissors?
examples.correct: Where are my scissors?

rules.title: "A pair of" changes the rule
rules.concept: If you add the phrase "A pair of" before scissors, spectacles, or trousers, the verb changes to singular.

examples.incorrect: A pair of shoes were bought by him.
examples.correct: A pair of shoes was bought by him.

rules.title: Nouns that look singular but are Plural
rules.concept: Words like Cattle, Clergy, Gentry, Poultry, Peasantry, Folk, People, Police look singular because they don't end in 's', but they are always plural and take a plural verb.

examples.incorrect: The cattle is grazing in the field.
examples.correct: The cattle are grazing in the field.

rules.title: Hyphenated Nouns cannot be plural
rules.concept: A noun used as a modifier with a hyphen must never be in plural form.

examples.incorrect: He gave me a five-rupees note.
examples.correct: He gave me a five-rupee note.

rules.title: Numbers + Noun of Measurement
rules.concept: When a definite number comes before words like Pair, Score, Dozen, Hundred, Thousand, Million, do not add 's' to them.

examples.incorrect: I bought two dozens bananas.
examples.correct: I bought two dozen bananas.

rules.title: Indefinite plural of measurement words
rules.concept: If words like hundred or dozen do not have a number before them, they can take an 's' along with the word "of".

examples.correct: Hundreds of people attended the rally.

rules.title: Noun + Preposition + Same Noun
rules.concept: When the exact same noun is repeated after a preposition, both nouns must be singular.

examples.incorrect: Rows upon rows of marble houses look beautiful.
examples.correct: Row upon row of marble houses looks beautiful.

rules.title: Words that don't change in Plural
rules.concept: Words like Deer, Sheep, Fish, Offspring have the exact same form in both singular and plural. Never write "sheeps".

examples.incorrect: I saw many sheeps in the meadow.
examples.correct: I saw many sheep in the meadow.

rules.title: Possession with Non-living things
rules.concept: Do not use apostrophe-s ('s) with non-living objects. Use the "of" structure instead.

examples.incorrect: The table's leg was broken.
examples.correct: The leg of the table was broken.

rules.title: Joint vs. Separate Possession
rules.concept: If two people own the same thing together, add 's to the last name only. If they own different things separately, add 's to both names.

examples.correct: Sham and Ram's joint account. (One account)
Sham's and Ram's cars. (Two different cars)

rules.title: Nouns ending in 's' sound (Hissing sound)
rules.concept: For singular nouns ending in a hissing 's' sound (Keats, Dickens, Jesus), just add an apostrophe (') at the end for possession, not another 's'.

examples.incorrect: Keats's poems are romantic.
examples.correct: Keats' poems are romantic.

rules.title: Compound Noun Plurals
rules.concept: To pluralize a compound noun, add 's' to the root/principal word, not the auxiliary words.

examples.incorrect: My brother-in-laws have arrived.
examples.correct: My brothers-in-law have arrived.

rules.title: "As regards" vs. "As regard"
rules.concept: The correct idiomatic phrase is always "as regards" or "in regard to". Never mix them up.

examples.incorrect: In regards to your letter...
examples.correct: In regard to your letter...

rules.title: Order of Personal Pronouns (Normal Situations)
rules.concept: When talking about general or good things, the order of pronouns must be 2nd Person (You) ➔ 3rd Person (He/She/They) ➔ 1st Person (I). (Trick: 231)

examples.incorrect: I, you and he will study together.
examples.correct: You, he and I will study together.

rules.title: Order of Personal Pronouns (Mistakes/Blame)
rules.concept: When confessing a mistake, crime, or guilt, the order switches to 1st Person (I) ➔ 2nd Person (You) ➔ 3rd Person (He/They). (Trick: 123)

examples.incorrect: You, he and I committed the crime.
examples.correct: I, you and he committed the crime.

rules.title: Comparison of Pronouns
rules.concept: Always compare the same cases. Subject pronouns are compared with subject pronouns (after words like "than" or "as").

examples.incorrect: He is faster than me.
examples.correct: He is faster than I (am).

rules.title: Pronouns after "Let" and Prepositions
rules.concept: Always use an object pronoun (me, him, her, us, them) after the word "Let" or after any preposition.

examples.incorrect: Let you and I solve this problem.
examples.correct: Let you and me solve this problem.

rules.title: Each other vs. One another
rules.concept: Use "Each other" when talking about two people. Use "One another" for more than two people.

examples.incorrect: The two brothers fought with one another.
examples.correct: The two brothers fought with each other.

rules.title: Who vs. Whom
rules.concept: Use Who when it acts as the subject performing the action (Replaceable with He/They). Use Whom when it acts as the object receiving the action (Replaceable with Him/Them).

examples.correct: Who wrote this letter? (He wrote it)
Whom did you invite? (You invited him)

rules.title: Relative Pronoun Match
rules.concept: The verb after who/which/that must match the noun directly before it (the antecedent).

examples.incorrect: It is I who is responsible.
examples.correct: It is I who am responsible. (Matches 'I')

rules.title: Use of "That" instead of "Who" or "Which"
rules.concept: Always use "That" after words like: All, Same, Only, Any, None, Little, Nothing and after Superlative adjectives.

examples.incorrect: This is the best book which I have ever read.
examples.correct: This is the best book that I have ever read.

rules.title: "Everybody / Everyone" Gender Tracking
rules.concept: When words like Everyone, Everybody, Each are used, track them using masculine singular pronouns (his/him) by default unless the gender is clearly female. Do not use "their".

examples.incorrect: Everyone should do their duty.
examples.correct: Everyone should do his duty.

rules.title: "One" must follow "One's"
rules.concept: If the subject of your sentence is the indefinite pronoun "One", you must use "one's" for possession throughout the sentence, not "his" or "their".

examples.incorrect: One must do his duty honestly.
examples.correct: One must do one's duty honestly.

rules.title: Avoid Reflexive Pronouns as Subjects
rules.concept: Words ending in -self (Myself, Himself, Yourself) cannot act as the subject of a sentence without a preceding noun or pronoun.

examples.incorrect: Myself am Dr. Roy.
examples.correct: I am Dr. Roy. / I myself am Dr. Roy.

rules.title: Prohibited Reflexive Pronouns
rules.concept: Do not use reflexive pronouns (myself, yourself) after verbs like: Keep, Break, Stop, Turn, Qualify, Bathe, Move, Hide.

examples.incorrect: He hid himself behind the heavy curtain.
examples.correct: He hid behind the heavy curtain.

rules.title: Mandatory Reflexive Pronouns
rules.concept: You must use a reflexive pronoun object after these verbs if no direct object is present: Avail, Adapt, Absent, Amuse, Resign, Reconcile, Enjoy, Exert.

examples.incorrect: He absented from the class yesterday.
examples.correct: He absented himself from the class yesterday.

rules.title: "It is..." structure case
rules.concept: When a pronoun follows constructions like "It is" or "It was", it must be in the subject case.

examples.incorrect: It was him who helped the poor old man.
examples.correct: It was he who helped the poor old man.

rules.title: Both can never be Negative
rules.concept: Do not use "not" with the word "Both". Instead, use "Neither".

examples.incorrect: Both of them did not go to school.
examples.correct: Neither of them went to school.

rules.title: Double Comparatives are Prohibited
rules.concept: Never use two comparative indicators (more and -er) together in the same modifier phrase.

examples.incorrect: He is more wiser than his younger brother.
examples.correct: He is wiser than his younger brother.

rules.title: Adjectives ending in "-ior"
rules.concept: Adjectives like Senior, Junior, Superior, Inferior, Prior, Preferable are followed by the preposition "to", never "than".

examples.incorrect: Milk is preferable than tea.
examples.correct: Milk is preferable to tea.

rules.title: Any other in Comparative Degree
rules.concept: When comparing an item to the rest of its own group using comparative degree, use the phrase "any other" to exclude it from the rest of the group.

examples.incorrect: Iron is more useful than any metal.
examples.correct: Iron is more useful than any other metal.

rules.title: As... as / So... as
rules.concept: Use "As... as" for positive sentences, and "So... as" or "As... as" for negative sentences. The adjective inside must be in its simple base form (positive degree).

examples.incorrect: He is as wiser as his father.
examples.correct: He is as wise as his father.

rules.title: Too... to structure
rules.concept: The combination "Too... to" carries a negative meaning by itself (meaning "so much that it is impossible"). Do not add another negative word like "not".

examples.incorrect: He is too weak not to walk.
examples.correct: He is too weak to walk. (Means he is so weak that he cannot walk)

rules.title: Position of "Enough"
rules.concept: The word "Enough" is placed after the adjective it describes, but before nouns.

examples.incorrect: He is enough wise to understand your trick.
examples.correct: He is wise enough to understand your trick.

rules.title: Much vs. Very
rules.concept: Use Very before simple base adjectives (Positive degree) and Present Participles (verb+ing). Use Much before comparative adjectives (Comparative degree) and Past Participles (verb-v3).

examples.correct: It is a very interesting book.
I am much interested in this structural project.

rules.title: Little vs. Few (The Essential Scale)
rules.concept: Few = Plural Countable Nouns (Books, Days). Little = Uncountable Nouns (Water, Milk, Knowledge).

examples.incorrect: There are less people today.
examples.correct: There are fewer people today.

rules.title: Meaning differences: A few / A little
rules.concept: Few/Little = Almost zero (Negative meaning). A few/A little = Some amount (Positive meaning). The few/The little = All that is remaining.

examples.correct: A little knowledge is a dangerous thing.

rules.title: Adverbs modify Verbs (Not Adjectives)
rules.concept: To describe an action (verb), use an adverb (usually ending in '-ly'), not a base adjective.

examples.incorrect: She speaks beautiful.
examples.correct: She speaks beautifully.

rules.title: Verbs of Sensation (The Exception)
rules.concept: Verbs of sensory perception (Taste, Smell, Feel, Sound, Look, Be, Become) take an adjective, not an adverb.

examples.incorrect: The food smells deliciously.
examples.correct: The food smells delicious.

rules.title: Hard vs. Hardly
rules.concept: Hard = With great effort / solid. Hardly = Scarcely / Almost not at all (Negative word).

examples.incorrect: He hardly worked and topped the exam.
examples.correct: He worked hard and topped the exam.

rules.title: Late vs. Lately
rules.concept: Late = Not on time. Lately = Recently (Used mostly in Present Perfect tense).

examples.correct: I have not seen him lately.

rules.title: Inversion with Negative Adverbs
rules.concept: When a sentence starts with a negative adverb like Hardly, Scarcely, Seldom, Barely, No sooner, the helping verb must come before the subject.

examples.incorrect: Seldom I have seen such a beautiful painting.
examples.correct: Seldom have I seen such a beautiful painting.

rules.title: Double Negatives are Prohibited
rules.concept: Do not use negative words like not or never in the same clause with words that already have a negative meaning, such as Hardly, Scarcely, Until, Unless, Forbid, Prohibit, Lest.

examples.incorrect: Unless you do not work hard, you will fail.
examples.correct: Unless you work hard, you will fail.

rules.title: Since / For with Perfect Tenses
rules.concept: When a time duration is given using Since (point in time) or For (period of time), use a Perfect Tense or Perfect Continuous Tense, never a simple continuous tense.

examples.incorrect: I am living here since five years.
examples.correct: I have been living here for five years.

rules.title: Two actions in the Past (Past Perfect Rule)
rules.concept: When two actions happened in the past, the older action takes the Past Perfect Tense (Had + V3). The more recent action takes the Simple Past Tense (V2).

examples.incorrect: The train departed before I reached the station.
examples.correct: The train had departed before I reached the station.

rules.title: Future Tense after Time/Condition Clauses
rules.concept: Do not use "will" or "shall" in clauses starting with conditional or time words like If, When, Before, After, Until, Unless, As soon as. Use Simple Present instead.

examples.incorrect: If it will rain, we will cancel the match.
examples.correct: If it rains, we will cancel the match.

rules.title: Conditional Clauses — Type 3 (Imaginary Past)
rules.concept: If the conditional clause uses "Had + V3", the main result clause must use "would have + V3".

examples.incorrect: If you worked hard, you would have passed the exam.
examples.correct: If you had worked hard, you would have passed the exam.

rules.title: Unfulfilled Wish / Imaginary Conditions
rules.concept: For imaginary or hypothetical sentences starting with I wish, If only, As though, always use the plural past verb "Were", regardless of whether the subject is singular or plural.

examples.incorrect: I wish I was a king.
examples.correct: I wish I were a king.

rules.title: It is high time...
rules.concept: Phrases like It is time, It is high time, It is about time must be followed by a subject and a verb in the Simple Past Tense (V2).

examples.incorrect: It is high time we start studying.
examples.correct: It is high time we started studying.

rules.title: "Lest" must follow "Should"
rules.concept: The conjunction "Lest" means "for fear that". It is strictly paired with the helping verb "Should". Do not add "not" to it.

examples.incorrect: Run fast lest you will miss the train.
examples.correct: Run fast lest you should miss the train.

rules.title: Habitual Actions / Universal Truths
rules.concept: General truths, scientific laws, and daily habits are always written in the Simple Present Tense, even if the reporting introduction is in the past.

examples.incorrect: Our teacher said that the earth revolved around the sun.
examples.correct: Our teacher said that the earth revolves around the sun.

rules.title: Stative Verbs (No "-ing" form)
rules.concept: Verbs of mental state, emotion, or ownership (Love, Hate, Know, Understand, Own, Belong, Possess) are generally not used in the continuous (-ing) form.

examples.incorrect: I am knowing the answer.
examples.correct: I know the answer.

rules.title: Gerund after "Look forward to"
rules.concept: The prepositional phrases Look forward to, Used to, With a view to, Addicted to, Devoted to must be followed by a Gerund (Verb+ing), not a base verb infinitive.

examples.incorrect: I am looking forward to meet you.
examples.correct: I am looking forward to meeting you.

rules.title: Split Infinitive Error
rules.concept: Do not place an adverb between the word "to" and the base verb (Infinitive). Put the adverb after the verb.

examples.incorrect: You need to carefully check the documents.
examples.correct: You need to check the documents carefully.

rules.title: Bare Infinitive after "Make, Let, Bid"
rules.concept: Verbs like Make, Let, Bid, Watch, Hear take a plain verb without "to" (Bare Infinitive) when used in the active voice.

examples.incorrect: He made me to cry.
examples.correct: He made me cry.

rules.title: Dangling Participles (Subject Misalignment)
rules.concept: An introductory participle clause (-ing phrase) must clearly align with the subject that follows it. If it doesn't, the sentence structure breaks down.

examples.incorrect: Walking in the park, a snake bit him. (Was the snake walking in the park?)
examples.correct: While he was walking in the park, a snake bit him.

rules.title: As soon as... No balancing word
rules.concept: Do not add "then" after using the introductory phrase "As soon as". A simple comma is enough.

examples.incorrect: As soon as the thief saw the police, then he ran away.
examples.correct: As soon as the thief saw the police, he ran away.

rules.title: Since as a Time Marker (Past vs Present Perfect)
rules.concept: When "since" acts as a time connection link: Clause after since ➔ Simple Past (V2). Main clause before since ➔ Present Perfect (Has/Have + V3).

examples.incorrect: Many things changed since he left the city.
examples.correct: Many things have changed since he left the city.

rules.title: Scarcely / Hardly... When
rules.concept: Always pair the introductory adverbs Hardly and Scarcely with "when" or "before". Never use "than".

examples.incorrect: Hardly had I arrived at the station than the train left.
examples.correct: Hardly had I arrived at the station when the train left.

rules.title: No Sooner... Than
rules.concept: The introductory comparative phrase "No sooner" must be paired with "than". Never use "then" or "when".

examples.incorrect: No sooner did I open the door when the bird flew out.
examples.correct: No sooner did I open the door than the bird flew out.

rules.title: Not only... But also (Balance Rule)
rules.concept: The phrases Not only and But also must be placed right before matching parts of speech (Parallel placement).

examples.incorrect: He not only lost his home but also his job.
examples.correct: He lost not only his home but also his job. (Both sit right before nouns)

rules.title: Although / Though... Yet
rules.concept: Conjunctions like Although or Though are paired either with "yet" or a simple comma. Never use "but".

examples.incorrect: Although he worked hard, but he failed.
examples.correct: Although he worked hard, yet he failed. / Although he worked hard, he failed.

rules.title: Between... And
rules.concept: The preposition "Between" is strictly paired with the conjunction "and". Never use "to".

examples.incorrect: Contact us between 10 AM to 5 PM.
examples.correct: Contact us between 10 AM and 5 PM.

rules.title: From... To
rules.concept: If you prefer to use the word "to" for a range, switch the introductory word from "between" to "From".

examples.correct: Contact us from 10 AM to 5 PM.

rules.title: "So... that" vs. "Too... to"
rules.concept: Do not mix up these two structures. It is either So + Adjective + That clause or Too + Adjective + To infinitive.

examples.incorrect: He is too weak that he cannot walk.
examples.correct: He is so weak that he cannot walk.

rules.title: Unless vs. Until
rules.concept: Until is tied to a Time threshold. Unless is tied to a Condition.

examples.correct: Wait here until I return. (Time)
You will fail unless you study. (Condition)

rules.title: Avoid "That" with Interrogative Sentences
rules.concept: In indirect speech, do not use the conjunction "that" before question words like Who, Which, What, Why, When, How, If, Whether.

examples.incorrect: He asked me that why I was late.
examples.correct: He asked me why I was late.

rules.title: "Whether" is paired with "Or"
rules.concept: When offering choices or showing doubt with options, use Whether... or. Do not use "if".

examples.incorrect: I do not know if he will come or not.
examples.correct: I do not know whether he will come or not.

rules.title: No Preposition after Transitive Verbs
rules.concept: Do not add prepositions after active verbs like Discuss, Enter, Marry, Order, Resemble, Comprise.

examples.incorrect: We discussed about the matter.
examples.correct: We discussed the matter.

rules.title: Enter vs. Enter into
rules.concept: Do not use "into" when walking physically inside a room or building. You can use "into" when entering agreements, alliances, or business deals.

examples.incorrect: He entered into the classroom.
examples.correct: He entered the classroom.

rules.title: Comprise vs. Consist of
rules.concept: The verb "Comprise" means consist of. Do not use the word "of" right after comprise in active voice sentences.

examples.incorrect: The book comprises of ten chapters.
examples.correct: The book comprises ten chapters. / The book consists of ten chapters.

rules.title: Died of vs. Died from
rules.concept: Use Died of for internal causes like diseases, hunger, or thirst (Died of cancer). Use Died from for external causes like overwork, wounds, or poison (Died from food poisoning).

examples.correct: He died of cholera.

rules.title: Angry with vs. Angry at
rules.concept: Use Angry with a person. Use Angry at a thing, action, or behavior.

examples.correct: I am angry with you, but I am angry at your behavior.

rules.title: Blind in vs. Blind to
rules.concept: Use Blind in when referring to physical loss of sight (Blind in the left eye). Use Blind to when someone ignores faults or mistakes (Blind to his son's mistakes).

examples.correct: A father should not be blind to his child's faults.

rules.title: Senior/Junior take "to"
rules.concept: As covered in Rule 47, Latin comparative adjectives never take "than".

examples.incorrect: He is junior than me.
examples.correct: He is junior to me.

rules.title: In vs. Into (State of Motion)
rules.concept: Use In to describe something that is already static inside a place. Use Into to show movement from the outside to the inside.

examples.correct: He is sitting in the room.
He jumped into the swimming pool.

rules.title: Beside vs. Besides
rules.concept: Beside = By the side of / next to. Besides = In addition to / apart from.

examples.incorrect: Sit besides me.
examples.correct: Sit beside me.

rules.title: Accompanied by vs. Accompanied with
rules.concept: Use Accompanied by for individuals/people, and Accompanied with for objects or things.

examples.correct: The PM was accompanied by his bodyguards.
Fever is often accompanied with a headache.

rules.title: Return / Revert back
rules.concept: The prefixes re- in words like Return, Revert, Retreat, Reimburse already mean "back". Adding the word "back" after them is repetitive and incorrect.

examples.incorrect: Please return back my book.
examples.correct: Please return my book.

rules.title: Reason why... because
rules.concept: The phrase "The reason why" already explains cause. Do not use the word "because" or "due to" later in the same statement. Use "that" instead.

examples.incorrect: The reason why he failed was because he didn't study.
examples.correct: The reason why he failed was that he didn't study.

rules.title: Supposing if
rules.concept: Both "Supposing" and "If" serve the exact same purpose to introduce a condition. Never use them right next to each other.

examples.incorrect: Supposing if it rains, what will we do?
examples.correct: If it rains, what will we do? / Supposing it rains, what will we do?

rules.title: Cousin brother / Cousin sister
rules.concept: The word "Cousin" includes both genders. Adding "brother" or "sister" after it is redundant in English grammar. Use context clues like he or she to show their gender.

examples.incorrect: She is my cousin sister.
examples.correct: She is my cousin.

rules.title: Final Conclusion / Twin Brothers
rules.concept: A conclusion is always final, and twins always come in pairs. Adding words like "final" or "twin" before them creates unnecessary repetition.

examples.incorrect: This is the final conclusion of our research project.
examples.correct: This is the conclusion of our research project.

questions.question: One of the most critical factors (A) / that determines the economic stability (B) / of a developing nation are its manufacturing output. (C) / No Error (D)
options: One of the most critical factors
of a developing nation are its manufacturing output.
questions.explanation: The true subject of the sentence is "One" (from the construction One of + Plural Noun). The relative clause "that determines..." modifies "factors", but the main verb of the sentence must agree with "One". Therefore, the plural verb "are" must be replaced with the singular verb "is".

questions.question: Neither the financial analysts (A) / nor the chief executive officer are optimistic (B) / about the market recovery in the upcoming fiscal quarter. (C) / No Error (D)
options: nor the chief executive officer are optimistic
about the market recovery in the upcoming fiscal quarter.
questions.explanation: When two subjects are connected using the correlative conjunction Neither...nor, the verb must agree with the subject closest to it. Here, the closest subject is "the chief executive officer" (singular). Thus, "are" must be changed to "is".

questions.question: A substantial body of evidence (A) / compiled by global climate scientists (B) / suggest that sea levels are rising faster than projected. (C) / No Error (D)
options: suggest that sea levels are rising faster than projected.
questions.explanation: The subject is the collective noun phrase "A substantial body" (singular), not the modifying object "evidence". A singular subject demands a singular verb form. Change "suggest" ($V_1$) to "suggests" ($V_5$).

questions.question: The dynamic variations in (A) / the temperature of the upper atmosphere (B) / is responsible for sudden changes in regional weather patterns. (C) / No Error (D)
options: the temperature of the upper atmosphere
is responsible for sudden changes in regional weather patterns.
questions.explanation: This is a classic "distortion by prepositional phrase" trap. The true subject is "variations" (plural). The phrase "in the temperature of the upper atmosphere" simply modifies it. Replace the singular verb "is" with the plural verb "are".

questions.question: The behavior of the local crowd (A) / during the protest rallies (B) / were highly unpredictable and caused panic among the residents. (C) / No Error (D)
options: The behavior of the local crowd
were highly unpredictable and caused panic among the residents.
questions.explanation: The subject is "behavior" (singular noun). The plural noun "rallies" is merely part of a modifying prepositional phrase. Change "were" to "was" to achieve proper grammatical agreement.

questions.question: Not only the students (A) / but also their accompanying class teacher (B) / were deeply concerned about the unexpected change in the syllabus. (C) / No Error (D)
options: but also their accompanying class teacher
were deeply concerned about the unexpected change in the syllabus.
questions.explanation: When using Not only...but also, the verb tracks the closest subject. Here, "class teacher" is singular. The plural verb "were" must be corrected to the singular "was".

questions.question: Knowledge of at least (A) / two core programming languages (B) / are mandatory for securing a software engineering role at the firm. (C) / No Error (D)
options: are mandatory for securing a software engineering role at the firm.
questions.explanation: The subject is the abstract noun "Knowledge" (uncountable and singular). The plural phrase "two core programming languages" can trick your eye because it sits next to the verb. Change "are" to "is".

questions.question: Each of the newly recruited candidates (A) / have been instructed to submit (B) / their original credentials before the end of the day. (C) / No Error (D)
options: Each of the newly recruited candidates
their original credentials before the end of the day.
questions.explanation: The pronoun "Each" is strictly singular and takes a singular verb. Change "have been" to "has been". (Bonus Error: "their" in part C should ideally be "his or her", though TCS frequently targets the verb element in these specific combinations).

questions.question: The prime minister, accompanied by (A) / several high-ranking cabinet ministers, (B) / have arrived at the international convention center. (C) / No Error (D)
options: have arrived at the international convention center.
questions.explanation: When a subject is joined with other nouns using phrases like accompanied by, along with, as well as, or together with, ignore the secondary nouns. The verb agrees solely with the first subject, "The prime minister" (singular). Change "have arrived" to "has arrived".

questions.question: A number of technical glitches (A) / was detected during the beta testing phase (B) / of the newly developed mobile application. (C) / No Error (D)
options: was detected during the beta testing phase
of the newly developed mobile application.
questions.explanation: A number of + Plural Noun $\rightarrow$ Takes a plural verb (means "many"). The number of + Plural Noun $\rightarrow$ Takes a singular verb (denotes a single specific figure). Since this sentence uses "A number of", change the singular "was" to the plural "were".

questions.question: The performance of our athletes (A) / in the recent international tournaments (B) / have fallen drastically short of public expectations. (C) / No Error (D)
options: have fallen drastically short of public expectations.
questions.explanation: The true grammatical subject is "performance" (singular). Do not let the plural noun "athletes" dictate the verb. Change "have fallen" to "has fallen".

questions.question: Two-thirds of the total wheat crop (A) / were ruined due to the unseasonal rainfall (B) / that lashed the northern plains last week. (C) / No Error (D)
options: Two-thirds of the total wheat crop
were ruined due to the unseasonal rainfall
that lashed the northern plains last week.
questions.explanation: For fractional or percentage expressions (two-thirds of, half of, most of), the verb is determined by the noun following the preposition "of". Here, "wheat crop" is singular and uncountable. Therefore, change "were" to "was".

questions.question: Every man, woman, and child (A) / in the flood-affected village (B) / were provided with emergency medical aid by the volunteers. (C) / No Error (D)
options: were provided with emergency medical aid by the volunteers.
questions.explanation: When a compound subject is preceded by the distributive adjective "Every" or "Each", the entire noun construction is treated as grammatically singular. Change "were" to "was".

questions.question: The heavy influx of foreign direct investment (A) / into the infrastructure sectors (B) / have stabilized the volatile national currency. (C) / No Error (D)
options: The heavy influx of foreign direct investment (A)
have stabilized the volatile national currency. (C)
questions.explanation: The true singular subject is "influx". The word "sectors" belongs to a qualifying prepositional phrase. Change "have" to "has".

questions.question: The quality of these newly manufactured (A) / electronic luxury items are not up to (B) / the rigorous international safety standards. (C) / No Error (D)
options: The quality of these newly manufactured (A)
electronic luxury items are not up to (B)
questions.explanation: The noun phrase "The quality" is singular and acts as the true subject. Replace the plural verb "are" with the singular "is".

questions.question: Many a prospective investor (A) / have sustained heavy losses (B) / due to the sudden crash of the unregulated cryptocurrency market. (C) / No Error (D)
options: due to the sudden crash of the unregulated cryptocurrency market. (C)
questions.explanation: The idiomatic phrase "Many a" takes a singular countable noun (investor) and structurally requires a singular verb. Change "have" to "has".

questions.question: The introduction of comprehensive reforms (A) / in the banking and financial sectors (B) / have yielded positive results within a short span. (C) / No Error (D)
options: in the banking and financial sectors (B)
have yielded positive results within a short span. (C)
questions.explanation: The true subject is "The introduction" (singular). The plural phrase "reforms in the banking and financial sectors" is an object of the preposition. Change "have" to "has".

questions.question: Rice and curry are the staple food (A) / of the majority of the population (B) / living in the coastal regions of the country. (C) / No Error (D)
options: Rice and curry are the staple food (A)
of the majority of the population (B)
living in the coastal regions of the country. (C)
questions.explanation: When two nouns are joined by "and" but express a single, combined, collective idea (like a single meal or concept: Rice and curry, Bread and butter, Slow and steady), they take a singular verb. Change "are" to "is".

questions.question: The accumulation of toxic industrial waste (A) / in the major urban rivers (B) / pose a severe threat to marine ecosystems. (C) / No Error (D)
options: The accumulation of toxic industrial waste (A)
pose a severe threat to marine ecosystems. (C)
questions.explanation: The singular subject "accumulation" demands a singular verb. Change the plural base verb "pose" to its singular variant "poses".

questions.question: Neither of the two configurations suggested (A) / by the technical engineering team (B) / are compatible with our current operating system. (C) / No Error (D)
options: Neither of the two configurations suggested (A)
are compatible with our current operating system. (C)
questions.explanation: "Neither" used as a pronoun refers to "none of the two" and is strictly singular. Change the plural verb "are" to "is".

questions.question: The data compiled by the research agency (A) / regarding the regional employment rates (B) / are highly inconsistent with official figures. (C) / No Error (D)
options: The data compiled by the research agency (A)
are highly inconsistent with official figures. (C)
questions.explanation: In modern standard English and competitive examinations, while "data" can be a plural collective, when treated as a singular mass entity compiled into a single report, it aligns with a singular verb. More explicitly, the structure focuses on the collection. Change "are" to "is".

questions.question: Three-quarters of the historic structure (A) / have been meticulously restored (B) / by the Archaeological Survey department. (C) / No Error (D)
questions.explanation: "Structure" is a singular singular entity. A fraction of a singular object remains singular. Replace "have been" with "has been".

questions.question: The major objective of the ongoing (A) / administrative and judicial interactions (B) / are to streamline the public grievance redressal mechanism. (C) / No Error (D)
options: The major objective of the ongoing (A)
are to streamline the public grievance redressal mechanism. (C)
questions.explanation: The subject is the singular noun "objective". Do not be confused by the plural adjective phrase "interactions". Change "are" to "is".

questions.question: Either the department head (A) / or his subordinate staff members (B) / is responsible for managing the daily operational logs. (C) / No Error (D)
options: is responsible for managing the daily operational logs. (C)
questions.explanation: When Either...or connects two subjects, the verb matches the closer subject. "staff members" is plural. Change the singular verb "is" to the plural "are".

questions.question: The severe outbreak of infectious viral diseases (A) / across the densely populated metropolitan regions (B) / were brought under control quickly. (C) / No Error (D)
options: The severe outbreak of infectious viral diseases (A)
across the densely populated metropolitan regions (B)
questions.explanation: The subject is "outbreak" (singular). "Diseases" and "regions" are nouns nested inside modifying phrases. Change "were" to "was".

questions.question: The defense attorney argued that (A) / his client was innocent because he (B) / had been out of the country since five years. (C) / No Error (D)
options: his client was innocent because he (B)
had been out of the country since five years. (C)
questions.explanation: This tests the Since vs. For rule. Since → Used for a specific fixed point in time (since 2015, since Monday). For → Used for a duration or total period of time (for 5 years, for 3 hours). Change "since" to "for".

questions.question: By the time the rescue team reached (A) / the remote landslide location, (B) / the local villagers already cleared the debris. (C) / No Error (D)
options: By the time the rescue team reached (A)
the local villagers already cleared the debris. (C)
questions.explanation: When two past actions happen sequentially, the earlier action must be expressed in the Past Perfect Tense (had + V3) and the later action in the Simple Past Tense (V2). The clearing of debris happened before the team arrived. Change "already cleared" to "had already cleared".

questions.question: For the past three consecutive months, (A) / the research team is working tirelessly (B) / on developing a stable synthetic vaccine strain. (C) / No Error (D)
options: For the past three consecutive months, (A)
the research team is working tirelessly (B)
on developing a stable synthetic vaccine strain. (C)
questions.explanation: If an action began in the past and is still ongoing in the present, accompanied by a time duration tag ("For the past three months"), you cannot use the Present Continuous tense. You must use the Present Perfect Continuous Tense. Change "is working" to "has been working".

questions.question: If the factory management (A) / would have taken timely safety precautions, (B) / the industrial disaster could have been avoided. (C) / No Error (D)
options: would have taken timely safety precautions, (B)
the industrial disaster could have been avoided. (C)
questions.explanation: This is a classic Type-3 Conditional sentence error. The structure for an unfulfilled past condition is: If + Past Perfect (had + V3), ... Would/Could have + V3. The "If-clause" cannot take "would have". Change "would have taken" to "had taken".

questions.question: As soon as the regulatory authority (A) / will issue the official clearance certificate, (B) / the construction work will resume immediately. (C) / No Error (D)
options: As soon as the regulatory authority (A)
will issue the official clearance certificate, (B)
the construction work will resume immediately. (C)
questions.explanation: In a future conditional or time-bound clause (introduced by words like As soon as, If, When, Until, Unless), you cannot use the future auxiliary "will" twice. The time/conditional clause must take the Simple Present Tense. Change "will issue" to "issues".

questions.question: The archeological department discovered (A) / that the ancient ruins contain (B) / inscriptions dating back to the Mauryan Empire. (C) / No Error (D)
options: inscriptions dating back to the Mauryan Empire. (C)
questions.explanation: If the principal clause is in the past tense ("discovered"), the subordinate clause must also match that past framing, unless it states a universal, permanent scientific truth. The inscriptions within the ruins are historical facts. Change "contain" to "contained".

questions.question: I have passed the competitive examination (A) / three years ago, but I have not received (B) / any official appointment letter yet. (C) / No Error (D)
options: I have passed the competitive examination (A)
three years ago, but I have not received (B)
questions.explanation: A sentence containing a specific past time marker or anchor point ("three years ago") cannot accept the Present Perfect Tense. It must take the Simple Past tense. Change "have passed" to "passed".

questions.question: Since she joined the corporate firm (A) / as a junior financial consultant, (B) / she is working with utmost dedication. (C) / No Error (D)
options: Since she joined the corporate firm (A)
she is working with utmost dedication. (C)
questions.explanation: When a sentence uses "Since + Simple Past clause" to mark a starting point, the main clause describing the ongoing action must be in the Present Perfect or Present Perfect Continuous tense. Change "is working" to "has been working".

questions.question: The general manager inquired (A) / whether anyone of the technical staff (B) / has completed the assigned project data entry. (C) / No Error (D)
options: whether anyone of the technical staff (B)
has completed the assigned project data entry. (C)
questions.explanation: Indirect speech rules apply here. Because the reporting verb is in the past tense ("inquired"), the present perfect "has completed" inside the indirect query must shift to the past perfect form. Change "has completed" to "had completed".

questions.question: If I was you, I would have (A) / rejected the unfair business proposal (B) / without any hesitation or second thoughts. (C) / No Error (D)
options: If I was you, I would have (A)
without any hesitation or second thoughts. (C)

questions.question: The standard physics textbook states (A) / that light traveled at a speed (B) / of approximately three lakh kilometers per second. (C) / No Error (D)
questions.explanation: Universal scientific laws or absolute facts are always stated in the Simple Present Tense, even if introduced by a past reporting framework (though here the introduction "states" is present anyway). Change "traveled" to "travels".

questions.question: We are living in this residential colony (A) / since our childhood, so we know (B) / all the local families living nearby. (C) / No Error (D)
questions.explanation: The presence of the time marker "since our childhood" indicates an action that started in the past and is still true. This blocks the Present Continuous tense. Change "We are living" to "We have been living".

questions.question: No sooner did the prime minister (A) / finished his independence day address (B) / than the heavy rain started pouring down. (C) / No Error (D)
questions.explanation: The auxiliary verb "did" must always be followed by the base form of the main verb ($V_1$). Combining "did" with the past-tense form "finished" creates a double-past infraction. Change "finished" to "finish".

questions.question: I will contact you (A) / the moment I will receive (B) / the updated confirmation from the operations department. (C) / No Error (D)
questions.explanation: The phrase "the moment" acts as a temporal conditional conjunction similar to "when". Do not use a future marker ("will") inside a time clause. Change "I will receive" to "I receive".

questions.question: The senior administrative officer (A) / had left the office premises (B) / an hour ago to attend a sudden inspection. (C) / No Error (D)
questions.explanation: The past time anchor "an hour ago" points to a specific point in time, requiring the Simple Past tense. The Past Perfect tense ("had left") is only used when ordering two relative past events. Change "had left" to "left".

questions.question: It is high time (A) / the government takes decisive regulatory measures (B) / to control the escalating prices of essential commodities. (C) / No Error (D)
questions.explanation: Phrasal idioms like It is time, It is high time, or It is about time must be followed by a clause in the Simple Past Tense ($V_2$) when indicating that an action is overdue. Change "takes" to "took".

questions.question: She confessed that she (A) / did not saw the warning signboard (B) / posted near the deep excavation zone. (C) / No Error (D)
questions.explanation: The negative past auxiliary "did not" must be paired with the base form of the verb ($V_1$). Using the past form "saw" is incorrect. Change "did not saw" to "did not see".

questions.question: The experienced mariner claimed (A) / that he traversed across the Atlantic Ocean (B) / more than ten times throughout his long career. (C) / No Error (D)
questions.explanation: Because the traversing happened prior to his past claim, this action requires the Past Perfect tense to establish clear chronological order. Change "he traversed" to "he had traversed".

questions.question: My father told me yesterday (A) / that honesty was always (B) / the best policy in any professional career. (C) / No Error (D)
questions.explanation: Proverbs, idioms, and universal moral truths never shift out of the Simple Present Tense, even when embedded within a past-tense reporting framework. Change "was" to "is".

questions.question: Until you do not complete (A) / the mandatory security documentation work, (B) / your account access will remain suspended. (C) / No Error (D)
questions.explanation: The temporal conjunction "Until" is inherently negative (meaning up to the time that not). Adding "do not" inside the clause creates a grammatically incorrect double negative. Change "Until you do not complete" to "Until you complete".

questions.question: The dynamic stock broker (A) / had buyed the high-performing shares (B) / just before the quarterly market rally began. (C) / No Error (D)
questions.explanation: This targets irregular past participle verb forms. The past participle ($V_3$) of the verb buy is bought, not the non-existent regularized form "buyed". Change "buyed" to "bought".

questions.question: When the fire alarm rang, (A) / the employees were found to be (B) / already left the commercial building. (C) / No Error (D)
questions.explanation: The action of leaving happened before the alarm check was noted. To show the completed state of a past action, use the perfect infinitive "to have left". Change "to be already left" to "to have already left".

questions.question: He told his close friends (A) / that he is preparing for the upcoming (B) / civil services examinations with focus. (C) / No Error (D)
questions.explanation: Indirect narration sequence trap. The reporting verb is in the past tense ("told"), which forces the present continuous "is preparing" to backshift into the Past Continuous Tense. Change "is preparing" to "was preparing".

questions.question: The historic treaty is signed (A) / by the representatives of both nations (B) / in Paris on the tenth of October, 1999. (C) / No Error (D)
questions.explanation: A specific year in the past ("1999") requires a past tense framework. Since the action is passive, use the Simple Past Passive structure ($was/were + V_3$). Change the present "is signed" to "was signed".

questions.question: Supposing if it rains heavily (A) / on the day of the exam, (B) / will the scheduled session be postponed? (C) / No Error (D)
questions.explanation: The words "Supposing" and "If" both express a conditional hypothesis. Using them side-by-side creates a redundant construction. Remove "if" or "supposing" to correct the sentence syntax.

questions.question: Of the two highly competitive engineering solutions (A) / proposed by the technical consultants, (B) / this option is definitely the best. (C) / No Error (D)
questions.explanation: When comparing exactly two things, you must use the comparative degree (better), not the superlative degree (best). Superlative degrees are reserved for comparisons involving three or more entities. Change "the best" to "the better".

questions.question: She is growing wiser and wiser (A) / but her sister is progressively becoming (B) / more taller every single day. (C) / No Error (D)
questions.explanation: This contains a double comparative error. "Taller" is already a comparative adjective. Adding the modifier "more" before it is grammatically redundant. Change "more taller" to "taller".

questions.question: The air pollution index of Delhi (A) / is significantly worse than (B) / any other metropolitan city in neighboring countries. (C) / No Error (D)
questions.explanation: This is an illogical comparison trap. The sentence mistakenly compares the pollution index of Delhi directly to a city (metropolitan city) instead of comparing it to the pollution index of that city. Change "than any other" to "than that of any other" (where "that of" refers back to the index).

questions.question: This antique wooden furniture is (A) / the most unique piece (B) / currently on display in the national museum. (C) / No Error (D)
questions.explanation: Adjectives like unique, perfect, absolute, complete, universal, ideal, or dead represent a superlative state inherent to their meaning. They cannot be graded or modified with words like "more" or "most". Change "the most unique" to "a unique".

questions.question: The newly appointed regional manager (A) / is senior and more experienced than (B) / any of the working executives in this department. (C) / No Error (D)
questions.explanation: When two adjectives requiring different prepositions are joined in a single sentence, both prepositions must be explicitly written. The adjective "senior" requires the preposition to, while "experienced" requires than. Change "is senior and more experienced than" to "is senior to and more experienced than".

questions.question: Little knowledge of medicinal herbs (A) / that he possessed proved to be an absolute lifesaver (B) / during the remote wilderness expedition. (C) / No Error (D)
questions.explanation: Little = Almost nothing (negative meaning).

questions.question: Can you please hand over (A) / any books on microeconomics (B) / that you can spare from your library? (C) / No Error (D)
options: that you can spare from your library? (C)
questions.explanation: In polite, affirmative requests or offers where we expect a positive answer, we use the adjective "some" instead of "any". "Any" is strictly reserved for negative or general interrogative structures. Change "any books" to "some books".

questions.question: Out of all the dynamic sectors, (A) / the technological domain is the most preferred (B) / and junior than the finance division. (C) / No Error (D)
options: Out of all the dynamic sectors, (A)
the technological domain is the most preferred (B)
and junior than the finance division. (C)
questions.explanation: Latin adjectives ending in -ior (like junior, senior, inferior, superior, prior) must always be followed by the preposition to, never the conjunction "than". Change "junior than" to "junior to".

questions.question: The performance of the young prodigy (A) / was relative better than (B) / what the critics had initially predicted. (C) / No Error (D)
options: The performance of the young prodigy (A)
what the critics had initially predicted. (C)
questions.explanation: Adjectives like comparatively or relatively inherently mean you are comparing values. Therefore, they must always be paired with a positive degree adjective, never a comparative one. Change "relative better" to "relatively good" or remove "relative".

questions.question: No lower than fifty prospective candidates (A) / turned up at the administrative office (B) / to submit their application forms. (C) / No Error (D)
options: No lower than fifty prospective candidates (A)
turned up at the administrative office (B)
questions.explanation: Less/Lower = Modifies uncountable mass quantities. Fewer = Modifies plural countable items. Since "candidates" can be counted, change "No lower than" to "No fewer than".

questions.question: The property developer clearly stated (A) / that the interior layout of the first house (B) / was preferable than the second one. (C) / No Error (D)
options: that the interior layout of the first house (B)
was preferable than the second one. (C)
questions.explanation: The adjective "preferable" inherently contains a comparative value and must be paired with the preposition to, not "than". Change "preferable than" to "preferable to".

questions.question: He behaves in a cowardly manner (A) / which makes him highly unsuited (B) / for a high-risk operational role in the armed forces. (C) / No Error (D)
options: He behaves in a cowardly manner (A)
for a high-risk operational role in the armed forces. (C)
questions.explanation: This sentence is No Error. TCS often tries to confuse students with words like cowardly, miserly, friendly, or brotherly. These words are adjectives, not adverbs. To modify the verb "behaves," the phrase "in a cowardly manner" is structurally flawless.

questions.question: The judicial committee remarked that (A) / the evidence produced by the prosecution (B) / was the most complete truth. (C) / No Error (D)
options: the evidence produced by the prosecution (B)
questions.explanation: Much like "unique", the adjective "complete" represents an absolute boundary condition. It cannot take comparative or superlative modifiers like "most". Change "the most complete truth" to "the complete truth".

questions.question: This particular segment of the highway (A) / is more safer for night driving (B) / compared to the alternative mountain route. (C) / No Error (D)
options: This particular segment of the highway (A)
is more safer for night driving (B)
compared to the alternative mountain route. (C)
questions.explanation: "Safer" is already in the comparative degree. Adding "more" introduces a redundant double comparative infraction. Change "more safer" to "safer".

questions.question: The new luxury sedan is (A) / five times more expensive than (B) / the older model currently running on roads. (C) / No Error (D)
options: the older model currently running on roads. (C)
questions.explanation: When multi-fold mathematical expressions like "times" are introduced for direct comparison, standard syntax rules prefer the absolute matching phrase format: "X times as [Positive Degree] as", rather than using the comparative more than. Change "five times more expensive than" to "five times as expensive as".

questions.question: My father is explicitly clear (A) / that he prefers reading classic literature (B) / rather than watching contemporary web series. (C) / No Error (D)
options: that he prefers reading classic literature (B)
rather than watching contemporary web series. (C)
questions.explanation: The verb "prefer" takes the preposition "to" when comparing two nouns or gerunds ($V_4$). Change "rather than watching" to "to watching".

questions.question: He did not bring any valid identification (A) / along with him to the examination hall, (B) / so he was denied entry by the supervisors. (C) / No Error (D)
options: He did not bring any valid identification (A)
along with him to the examination hall, (B)
so he was denied entry by the supervisors. (C)
questions.explanation: The sentence is No Error. The negative modifier "did not" is properly paired with the adjective "any".

questions.question: The weather condition today (A) / is comparatively hotter than it was (B) / during the exact same period last week. (C) / No Error (D)
options: is comparatively hotter than it was (B)
during the exact same period last week. (C)
questions.explanation: The modifier "comparatively" cannot be paired with a comparative adjective (hotter) because it creates a structural redundancy. Change "comparatively hotter" to "comparatively hot".

questions.question: Radha is cleverer than (A) / any student in her competitive (B) / batch at the coaching institute. (C) / No Error (D)
questions.explanation: When comparing a single individual to an entire group using a comparative degree, you must exclude that individual from the rest of the group by adding the word "other". Otherwise, Radha would be compared to a group that includes herself. Change "any student" to "any other student".

questions.question: The project manager assured that (A) / the task would be completed (B) / without any further delays. (C) / No Error (D)
questions.explanation: The sentence is No Error. "Further" means additional distance in degree or time, which is exactly what is intended here, as opposed to "farther," which measures physical geographic distance.

questions.question: Whole the country mourned the sudden (A) / demise of the highly respected (B) / senior military commander. (C) / No Error (D)
options: Whole the country mourned the sudden (A)
questions.explanation: The definite article "The" must be placed before the adjective "whole". The correct structural ordering is "The whole country", not "Whole the country". (Conversely, "all" takes the article after it: "All the countries").

questions.question: He does not have many money (A) / to invest in speculative capital ventures (B) / at this current juncture in his career. (C) / No Error (D)
options: He does not have many money (A)
to invest in speculative capital ventures (B)
at this current juncture in his career. (C)
questions.explanation: "Money" is an uncountable noun in English grammar. The modifier "many" can only be paired with countable nouns. Change "many money" to "much money" or "a lot of money".

questions.question: This branch of the banyan tree (A) / is much more longer than (B) / the one hanging over our residential roof. (C) / No Error (D)
options: This branch of the banyan tree (A)
the one hanging over our residential roof. (C)
questions.explanation: "Longer" is a comparative adjective. Adding "more" creates an incorrect double comparative. Note that using "much" as an intensive modifier before a comparative adjective (much longer) is perfectly valid, but "more" is incorrect. Change "much more longer" to "much longer".

questions.question: The creative design layout of this building (A) / is superior and more aesthetically pleasing than (B) / the colonial architecture of the old town hall. (C) / No Error (D)
options: The creative design layout of this building (A)
is superior and more aesthetically pleasing than (B)
the colonial architecture of the old town hall. (C)
questions.explanation: The adjective "superior" requires the fixed preposition "to". Change the segment to read: "is superior to and more aesthetically pleasing than".

questions.question: Solon is the most wisest man (A) / who has ever laid down administrative laws (B) / for this ancient civilization. (C) / No Error (D)
options: Solon is the most wisest man (A)
who has ever laid down administrative laws (B)
questions.explanation: "Wisest" is already a superlative adjective. Adding "most" creates an invalid double superlative. Change "the most wisest" to "the wisest".

questions.question: Seldom or ever have I witnessed (A) / such an incredibly emotional performance (B) / by a classical theater artist on stage. (C) / No Error (D)
options: Seldom or ever have I witnessed (A)
by a classical theater artist on stage. (C)
questions.explanation: This targets standard idiomatic adverbial pairings. The correct combinations are either "Seldom or never" or "Seldom, if ever". Mixing them into "Seldom or ever" is grammatically incorrect. Change "Seldom or ever" to "Seldom or never".

questions.question: Hardly had the train arrived (A) / at the platform than the passengers (B) / began to rush violently toward the compartments. (C) / No Error (D)
options: at the platform than the passengers (B)
began to rush violently toward the compartments. (C)

questions.question: No sooner the match had started (A) / when it began to rain heavily, forcing (B) / the players to run off the open field. (C) / No Error (D)
options: No sooner the match had started
when it began to rain heavily, forcing
the players to run off the open field.
questions.explanation: This sentence contains two major errors often tested by TCS. First, beginning a sentence with the negative adverb "No sooner" mandates adverbial inversion (the auxiliary verb must sit before the subject). Second, "No sooner" pairs with than, not "when". Change the first part to "No sooner had the match started than".

questions.question: The investigative journalist spoke (A) / in a highly brave manner about the systemic (B) / corruption deep within the administrative machinery. (C) / No Error (D)
options: in a highly brave manner about the systemic
corruption deep within the administrative machinery.
questions.explanation: The sentence is No Error. "Brave" can be converted into the adverb "bravely", but using the expanded descriptive phrase "in a highly brave manner" is also completely valid.

questions.question: He is rich enough (A) / to buy a premium luxury apartment (B) / in the most expensive locality of metropolitan Mumbai. (C) / No Error (D)
options: to buy a premium luxury apartment
in the most expensive locality of metropolitan Mumbai.
questions.explanation: The sentence is No Error. The adverb "enough" follows a specific positioning rule: it must always be placed after the adjective it modifies ("rich" is an adjective, so "rich enough" is correct). (Note: It precedes nouns, e.g., "enough money").

questions.question: The examination was so difficult (A) / that I was only able to solve (B) / two questions completely during the test. (C) / No Error (D)
options: that I was only able to solve
two questions completely during the test.
questions.explanation: The adverb "only" must be placed immediately before the word it modifies to avoid ambiguity. Here, it is meant to modify the quantity "two questions", not the ability to solve them. Change the segment to: "to solve only two questions".

questions.question: Scarcely the inspector had stepped out (A) / of his official police vehicle when (B) / a sudden gunshot echoed through the narrow alleyway. (C) / No Error (D)
options: Scarcely the inspector had stepped out
of his official police vehicle when
a sudden gunshot echoed through the narrow alleyway.
questions.explanation: Because the sentence begins with the restrictive adverb "Scarcely", you must use subject-auxiliary inversion. Shift the auxiliary verb "had" before the subject "the inspector". Change to: "Scarcely had the inspector stepped out".

questions.question: Under no circumstances (A) / the security personnel will allow (B) / unauthorized individuals to enter the high-security vault. (C) / No Error (D)
options: unauthorized individuals to enter the high-security vault.
questions.explanation: Prepositional phrases acting as negative restrictors (such as Under no circumstances, On no account, In no way) force an inversion if placed at the very start of a sentence. Change "the security personnel will allow" to "will the security personnel allow".

questions.question: He is too intelligent (A) / to not understand the hidden implications (B) / behind the diplomat's carefully worded statement. (C) / No Error (D)
options: to not understand the hidden implications
behind the diplomat's carefully worded statement.
questions.explanation: The core structural framework "Too...to" inherently carries a negative meaning (meaning so intelligent that he will definitely understand or too heavy to lift = so heavy that it cannot be lifted). Adding a secondary "not" creates an unintended double negative. Change "to not understand" to "to understand".

questions.question: Not only did she clear the preliminary exam, (A) / but she also topped the final interview (B) / with record-breaking marks. (C) / No Error (D)
options: Not only did she clear the preliminary exam,
but she also topped the final interview
questions.explanation: The sentence is No Error. When "Not only" starts a sentence, it triggers a valid inversion ("did she clear"), and it is properly balanced by "but she also" in the later clause.

questions.question: The corporate trainees were running (A) / too fastly to catch up with (B) / the senior fitness instructor during the drill. (C) / No Error (D)
options: too fastly to catch up with
the senior fitness instructor during the drill.
questions.explanation: The word "fastly" does not exist in standard English grammar. "Fast" functions as both an adjective and an adverb. Change "too fastly" to "too fast".

questions.question: He was uncommonly wise (A) / and handled the highly tense diplomatic crisis (B) / very masterly. (C) / No Error (D)
options: and handled the highly tense diplomatic crisis
questions.explanation: "Masterly" is an adjective (meaning characteristic of a master), not an adverb. To modify the verb "handled", you must use an adverbial construction. Change "very masterly" to "in a masterly manner".

questions.question: Never before I have seen (A) / such a spectacular display of fireworks (B) / during the annual festive celebrations. (C) / No Error (D)
options: such a spectacular display of fireworks
questions.explanation: Starting a sentence with the negative time adverb phrase "Never before" requires an inversion of the auxiliary verb and subject. Change "I have seen" to "have I seen".

questions.question: The financial auditor found that (A) / the company accounts had been managed (B) / in a quite dishonest way. (C) / No Error (D)
options: the company accounts had been managed
questions.explanation: The adverb "quite" must precede any indefinite articles (a/an) when modifying an adjective-noun unit. The correct structural sequence is "quite a dishonest way", not "in a quite dishonest way".

questions.question: She was so heavily shocked (A) / by the news of the sudden accident (B) / that she could barely speak a word. (C) / No Error (D)
options: by the news of the sudden accident
that she could barely speak a word.
questions.explanation: While "heavily" modifies physical items or actions (e.g., raining heavily), emotional or psychological states are modified by adverbs like deeply, profoundly, or severely. Change "heavily shocked" to "deeply shocked".

questions.question: Little he realized that (A) / the administrative decision would have (B) / such a catastrophic impact on his career. (C) / No Error (D)
options: such a catastrophic impact on his career.
questions.explanation: When the restrictive adverb "Little" is placed at the start of a sentence to emphasize a lack of awareness, it triggers an inversion. Since the context is simple past ("realized"), use the auxiliary "did". Change to: "Little did he realize".

questions.question: The operational guidelines provided by (A) / the defense headquarters are (B) / too much painful to implement on the ground. (C) / No Error (D)
options: too much painful to implement on the ground.
questions.explanation: This targets a nuanced adverbial modifier distinction: "Too much" is followed directly by a Noun (e.g., too much pain). "Much too" is followed directly by an Adjective (e.g., much too painful). Since "painful" is an adjective, change "too much painful" to "much too painful".

questions.question: He worked hardly throughout the year, (A) / which is why he failed to secure (B) / a passing score in the final Tier-2 evaluation. (C) / No Error (D)
options: He worked hardly throughout the year,
which is why he failed to secure
a passing score in the final Tier-2 evaluation.
questions.explanation: Hard = With great effort and energy (positive meaning). Hardly = Barely/Almost not at all (negative meaning). The sentence context explains why he failed, indicating he put in almost no effort. Therefore, the placement of "hardly" is logically correct, but its position is wrong. "Hardly" should precede the verb it modifies. Change to "He hardly worked throughout the year".

questions.question: No sooner had the alarm rung (A) / then he jumped out of bed (B) / and started preparing for his morning shift. (C) / No Error (D)
options: No sooner had the alarm rung
then he jumped out of bed
and started preparing for his morning shift.
questions.explanation: "No sooner" must be followed by the conjunction "than". TCS frequently slips in the time marker "then" as a visual trap. Change "then" to "than".

questions.question: The project was finished (A) / clean and completely within (B) / the tight deadline allocated by the client. (C) / No Error (D)
options: the tight deadline allocated by the client.
questions.explanation: To modify the passive verb construction "was finished", you must use a proper adverb. "Clean" is an adjective. Change it to the adverb "cleanly" or remove it to avoid redundancy with "completely".

questions.question: Only by working hard (A) / you can achieve your dream (B) / of becoming an Income Tax Inspector. (C) / No Error (D)
options: of becoming an Income Tax Inspector.
questions.explanation: When a sentence begins with a restrictive phrase starting with "Only" (such as Only by, Only when, Only after), the main clause that follows must undergo subject-auxiliary inversion. Change "you can achieve" to "can you achieve".

questions.question: The water of the holy river (A) / was direct flowing into (B) / the deep concrete reservoir channels. (C) / No Error (D)
options: The water of the holy river
questions.explanation: To modify the continuous verb action "flowing", you must use an adverb rather than an adjective. Change "direct" to "directly".

questions.question: I am directly coming (A) / from the administrative office (B) / to clear all your pending doubts. (C) / No Error (D)
options: to clear all your pending doubts.
questions.explanation: When expressing immediate sequential movement in time or space, standard idiom usage prefers the adverb "straight" over "directly" to avoid ambiguity regarding physical trajectory. Change "directly coming" to "coming straight".

questions.question: He was remarkably optimal (A) / about his selection prospects, (B) / despite facing multiple setbacks in the past. (C) / No Error (D)
options: despite facing multiple setbacks in the past.
questions.explanation: This is an incorrect word choice trap. "Optimal" means the best or most favorable condition for a process. The sentence describes a psychological state of hopefulness, which requires the adjective "optimistic". Change "optimal" to "optimistic".

questions.question: Not until the entire country (A) / was locked down the citizens (B) / realized the severe intensity of the viral pandemic. (C) / No Error (D)
options: realized the severe intensity of the viral pandemic.
questions.explanation: When a sentence begins with a negative time constraint phrase like "Not until...", the inversion does not happen in the initial "until" clause itself; it is triggered in the main governing clause that follows. Change "the citizens realized" (simple past) to " did the citizens realize".

questions.question: The board of directors were divided (A) / in their opinions regarding the appointment (B) / of the new managing director. (C) / No Error (D)
options: The board of directors were divided
in their opinions regarding the appointment
questions.explanation: This sentence is No Error. When a collective noun (board of directors, jury, committee) is divided or acts as individuals, it takes a plural verb (were) and a plural pronoun (their). This is grammatically perfect.

questions.question: Every employee must bring (A) / their own laptop to the workshop (B) / as per the new IT policy guidelines. (C) / No Error (D)
options: their own laptop to the workshop
as per the new IT policy guidelines.
questions.explanation: The distributive pronoun "Every" is singular and must be paired with singular tracking pronouns. Change "their own laptop" to "his or her own laptop".

questions.question: Between you and I, (A) / the newly proposed tax structure (B) / is highly unfavorable to small business owners. (C) / No Error (D)
options: is highly unfavorable to small business owners.
questions.explanation: Prepositions like between, except, like, or but must always be followed by a pronoun in the objective case. Change "Between you and I" to "Between you and me".

questions.question: The candidate whom we thought (A) / would easily secure the top rank (B) / failed to clear even the Tier-1 cutoff. (C) / No Error (D)
options: would easily secure the top rank
failed to clear even the Tier-1 cutoff.
questions.explanation: This is a classic Who vs. Whom trap. If you remove the parenthetical phrase "we thought," the relative pronoun acts as the direct subject for the verb phrase "would easily secure." Therefore, it must be in the subjective case. Change "whom" to "who".

questions.question: It was me who telephoned (A) / the emergency helpline number (B) / when the fire broke out in the building. (C) / No Error (D)
options: when the fire broke out in the building.
questions.explanation: When a pronoun follows a form of the "to be" verb serving as an identifier (is, was, were), it must be in the subjective case. Change "It was me" to "It was I".

questions.question: He is one of those technical experts (A) / who never compromises on the structural (B) / integrity of architectural designs. (C) / No Error (D)
options: He is one of those technical experts
who never compromises on the structural
questions.explanation: When a relative pronoun (who, which, that) connects a clause, its verb agrees with its immediate antecedent. Here, the antecedent is the plural noun "experts," making the relative clause plural. Change "compromises" to "compromise".

questions.question: The two business partners frequently (A) / argued with one another over (B) / the allocation of corporate profits. (C) / No Error (D)
questions.explanation: Use "each other" when referring strictly to two entities. "One another" is reserved for three or more entities. Change "one another" to "each other".

questions.question: Myself am responsible (A) / for executing this entire project (B) / within the specified budget guidelines. (C) / No Error (D)
questions.explanation: A reflexive pronoun (myself, himself, yourself) can never function as the primary subject of a sentence without an accompanying subjective pronoun. Change "Myself am" to "I myself am" or simply "I am".

questions.question: The master craftsman was deeply annoyed (A) / at his apprentice forgetting (B) / to lock the tool shed overnight. (C) / No Error (D)
options: The master craftsman was deeply annoyed
to lock the tool shed overnight.
questions.explanation: A noun or pronoun modifying a gerund ($V_4$ acting as a noun, like forgetting) must always be in the possessive case. Change "at his apprentice forgetting" to "at his apprentice's forgetting".

questions.question: This luxury sedan is (A) / far superior to that (B) / manufactured by our competitor firm. (C) / No Error (D)
questions.explanation: This is a pronoun-based faulty comparison trap. The sentence should compare a sedan to another sedan's traits, or use a pronoun demonstrative to balance the structure. Change "to that" to "to that one" or "to the one".

questions.question: You, he and I (A) / must coordinate effectively to complete (B) / this project assignment by tomorrow evening. (C) / No Error (D)
options: this project assignment by tomorrow evening.
